/.title: Tauira
/.content:
## Tauira — Autoethnographic Knowledge Graph

**Tauira** maps the entanglements of a collaborative classroom as a living rhizomatic network. Each node is a participant — Material, Knowledge, or Instinctual — and each edge records a relational force between them across encounters.

> Explore encounters in the sidebar, or open the [Rhizomatic Map]({{< relref "/map" >}}) to navigate by term.

/artefacts/.title: Artefacts
/artefacts/.content: Learning artefacts — lesson plans, worksheets, reflective template, and classroom documents referenced across encounters.

/artefacts/artefact-001.title: Artefact 001 — Critical Incident Report - Encounter One
/artefacts/artefact-001.content:
## Summary of Critical Incident

The last activity of the lesson on “Affordance” required students to transfer their knowledge of the principles of Affordance to designing a product. Initially, students engaged well with prior knowledge activation and affordance scanning, but as tasks shifted to critical analysis and creative application, I noticed damp energy in discussions. I felt uneasy owing to my fact-heavy structure, which cultivated intellect effectively, but neglected emotional connection. I recognised the challenge to integrate love—empathy, relational warmth—with reason for acquiring and using knowledge.

##  Context

This incident occurred during the final activity of the lesson with IBDP Psychology students.  

## Wider Influences

My realisation of intellect-love imbalance has brought to my awareness the challenges associated with it. Nel Noddings' care ethics (1984, Caring) posits education as a relational act where teachers prioritise "caring-for" through engrossment and motivational displacement, shifting from abstract knowledge transference to authentic, personalised connections that are embedded in learners' lived realities. In my lesson, this critique fact-heavy tasks for neglecting the relatedness needed to perceive emotional affordances.Jiddu Krishnamurti (1970s dialogues, Education and the Significance of Life) urges choiceless awareness. The reason is detached from conditioning and is integrated with love as a unified perception. Rejecting fragmented intellect cultivation for direct seeing (perceiving) resonates with ecological affordance's unmediated organism-environment mutuality. This incident has made me aware of my own learning experiences that are fact-heavy. Furthermore, I see learning not as a collection of facts and objects, but a meaning-making process that gives structure to our lives. 

## Application to professional practice: 

This incident reveals an affective challenge: balancing curriculum demands (e.g., critical evaluation of research) with learners' humanity.  The former risks superficial engagement. Future lessons will integrate love-reason before theory. For instance, gallery walks will include peer empathy feedback. As Palmer (1998) states, "Good teaching comes from the identity and integrity of the teacher," so I commit to relational routines. These routines will include discreet emotion prompts amid activities while ensuring replicable depth without stifling inquiry.  

## Related Teachers’ Standards

- **5c** — Demonstrate awareness of the physical, social, and intellectual development of learners, and adapt teaching to support them. 
- **1c** — Demonstrate consistently the positive attitudes, values, and behaviour expected of pupils. 
- **1a** — Establish a safe and stimulating environment for pupils, rooted in mutual respect. 

## Self-Evaluation Assessment for Learning

The report records that **ALL** learners were able to describe affordance with evidence and **MOST** were able to analyse ecological versus cognitive perspectives.  At the same time, pair discussions revealed factual recall without emotional depth, and time-management notes indicated disengagement during evaluative stages. 

The report also notes that students’ creativity appeared in their abstracts, including novel ideas such as body-scaled BCI. Yet I also recognised my discomfort in “simply knowing” learner needs without relational dimensions, which limited holistic transfer. 
The proposed next step is to incorporate love-reason integration in future lessons, including journal activities and pre/post reflection on emotional-concept connections through exit feedback. 

## Rationale

The portfolio explicitly states that this self-evaluation follows Gibbs’ Reflective Cycle. The sequence of description, feelings, and evaluation is grounded in lesson observations, discomfort with disengagement, and evidence of factual success alongside emotional gaps.

Within Tauira, this is precisely what makes the artefact analytically useful. It offers a clear example of how prescribed reflection organizes pedagogical experience into a legible narrative of observation, feeling, evaluation, and future action, while also leaving open a richer diffractive rereading through the encounter and memo network. 

## Notes

- This artefact is an anonymised critical incident report from the Professional Development Portfolio. 
- Student names do not appear in the record. 
- The lesson centred on Affordance in IBDP Psychology and the final task required transfer from conceptual understanding to product design. 
- The portfolio frames the event through Gibbs’ Reflective Cycle, while Tauira extends it through assemblage analysis and rhizomatic mapping. 
- See [[enc-2025-T1-W3-L2]] for the encounter version of the event and [[memo-001]] for the diffractive memo that identifies further gaps, especially around time pressure and the ambiguity of the creative task.

/encounters/.title: Encounters
/encounters/.content: Classroom encounter records — primary data units of the Tauira autoethnographic knowledge graph.

/encounters/enc-2025-T1-W3-L2.title: Encounter One — The Slowing of the Room
/encounters/enc-2025-T1-W3-L2.content:
This encounter first appears as a familiar reflective problem: a transition did not work, and the teacher later identifies pacing as the issue. Through Kolb, Gibbs, or Schön, the event could be organized as observation, evaluation, and future adjustment. Yet in Tauira this encounter should not remain a closed lesson about technique.

Rhizomatically, the event links to recurring nodes across the project: analytic performance, material orientation, visible evidence, and the production of compliance. The encounter therefore matters less as a single failure of pacing than as one expression of a wider pattern in which pedagogical rigour, classroom objects, and evaluative pressure repeatedly thin relation. See also [[enc-2025-T1-W4-L1]] for the recurrence of visible evidence and institutional legitimacy, [[enc-2025-T1-W5-L3]] for the recurrence of affective shifts and role instability, and [[memo-001]] for the diffractive map of compliance-affect across encounters.

The worksheet-compliance pattern visible here resurfaces in [[enc-2025-T1-W5-L3]] and is theorised through Barad in [[memo-001]] and [[memo-003]]. The question of what counts as visible learning links this encounter to [[enc-2025-T1-W4-L1]] and its analysis in [[memo-002]].

/encounters/enc-2025-T1-W4-L1.title: Encounter Two — The Homework that Changed Shape
/encounters/enc-2025-T1-W4-L1.content:
This encounter can easily be narrated in reflective discourse as a successful act of differentiation. Kolb, Gibbs, and Schön all support that reading by helping the teacher convert the event into professional learning about flexibility. In Tauira, however, the event should remain open as a site where medium, legitimacy, and authority are redistributed.

Rhizomatically, this encounter connects to other nodes beyond differentiation: written legitimacy, assessment comfort, visible rigour, and the politics of medium. It is therefore not only about one student and one task. It belongs to a wider network in which writing repeatedly appears as the default carrier of seriousness, while alternative media expose the material-discursive preferences through which teacher authority is stabilised. See [[enc-2025-T1-W3-L2]] for the recurrence of visible evidence and analytic compliance, [[enc-2025-T1-W5-L3]] for the recurrence of role instability when the pedagogical frame is disturbed, and [[memo-002]] for the cross-encounter map of legitimacy, medium, and comfort.

The affective charge of recognition in this encounter connects to the affect patterns traced in [[memo-001]] and [[memo-003]]. The question of assessment legitimacy links forward to the concept-affect threshold in [[enc-2025-T1-W5-L3]] and is analysed through Massumi in [[memo-002]].

/encounters/enc-2025-T1-W5-L3.title: Encounter Three — The Sadness in the Room
/encounters/enc-2025-T1-W5-L3.content:
This encounter can be processed through familiar reflective theories as an instance of sensitive facilitation, reflection-in-action, or later professional learning about care. Those readings remain useful. But Tauira should hold the event as more than a lesson in better handling difficult topics.

Rhizomatically, this encounter links concept to affect, affect to temporality, and temporality to role instability. It therefore extends beyond the individual student response and becomes part of a wider map of how knowledge enters bodies, memories, and ethical relations. In this network, sadness is not outside learning. It is one of the ways the pedagogical assemblage makes learning happen. See [[enc-2025-T1-W3-L2]] for the recurrence of affective thinning and compliance in the room, [[enc-2025-T1-W4-L1]] for the earlier disturbance of teacher authority and role, and [[memo-003]] for the threshold map connecting concept, identity, and pedagogical tempo.

The worksheet-tempo pattern here echoes the material compliance of [[enc-2025-T1-W3-L2]], analysed in [[memo-001]]. The role instability in this encounter connects to the assessment authority unsettled in [[enc-2025-T1-W4-L1]] and theorised through Massumi in [[memo-002]] and [[memo-003]].

/essays/.title: Essays
/essays/.content: Essays — theoretical accounts synthesising encounter data for Module 7440 of the PGDEI  programme.

/essays/essay-001.title: Narrating Growth Diffractively
/essays/essay-001.content:
## Introduction

Reflection in professional practice, especially in educator education, is at a tipping point. In contemporary educator education, reflection often takes the form of evidence in prescribed post-lesson commentary. Such routines may support accountability and professional discipline, but they could also narrow what counts as learning (Schön, 1983; Gibbs, 1988; Bozalek and Zembylas, 2017). Over time, the routines become a script for how both professional and personal growth should be narrated. In this essay, I examine narrative scripting as the central aspect of reflection in my own professional practice.
This inquiry matters to me personally and professionally because it advances my progression as an educator-researcher, building on the modules and the wider PGDEI programme. The inquiry began with discomfort toward the convenience of prescribed reflective routines. This discomfort pushed me to ask not whether reflection matters, but what kind of reflection becomes possible when classroom life is approached as relational, affective, and materially entangled (Barad, 2007; Bozalek and Zembylas, 2017; Hill, 2017; Lambert, 2021). In this essay, I move beyond treating classroom encounters as a backdrop for retrospective self-improvement. Drawing on evidence and its analysis curated through Tauira, I argue that prescribed reflective practices should not exclusively document experience and that they regulate how professional growth could be narrated diffractively.

---

## Defining the Aspect

The aspect I examine here is the way prescribed reflection scripts professional and personal growth into a familiar story arc of criticism, adaptability, and improvement. Reflective templates not only invite educators to think but also organise how that thinking should appear. The educator is assumed to be a reflective, critical, progressive, ethical, and improving professional (Kolb, 1984; Gibbs, 1988; Schön, 1983), while the complexity of pedagogical life itself is reduced to docile afterthoughts on the performance of the educator.
Diffractive literature offers a pragmatic challenge to this logic. Barad (2007) argues that diffraction is not a mirror of sameness but is awareness of differing patterns produced through the entanglement of participants. Diffraction, a word adopted from physics by Karen Barad, is not the reflection of one thing in another. It is what happens when waves interact and produce an interference pattern that was not present in either wave alone (Barad, 2007). Then, a diffractive reading of the classroom encounters asks what pattern emerges at the point of interference between the lesson-as-designed and the lesson-as-lived? Developing on this, Bozalek and Zembylas (2017) contrast reflection with diffraction, arguing that reflection often assumes a bounded subject who looks back on experience, whereas diffraction attends to how bodies, discourses, materialities, and histories intra-act in the emergence of the classroom encounters. Hill (2017) extends this, in the education context, through the role of the diffractive practitioner. Meanwhile, Lambert (2021) and Nociti (2024) show how diffractive practice can edify educator learning in ways that exceed retrospective self-appraisal. Such a framework aligns with complex accounts of educator learning in which practice is not linear and individual but emergent, distributed, and shaped by multiple forces (Strom and Viesca, 2023).
Tauira is imperative here because it supports this essay and a diffractive inquiry. In my research project, Tauira is a website-based knowledge environment where encounters, fieldnotes, memos, artefacts, homework, essays, and interaction maps are gathered and revisited across practice over time. It is not simply a repository. It functions as a relation-disclosing object that allows pedagogical moments to be reread across bodies, objects, timings, space, affects, and media. Therefore, Tauira is not only evidence of my individual competence or growth.

---

## Context of Practice

The essay draws on encounters from my professional teaching practice, especially within IB MYP/DP Psychology lessons and portfolio-based reflection in the PGDEI programme. This context matters because it merges deep conceptual understanding with institutional expectations for evidence, progress, and reflective accountability. In such professional settings, there is strong pressure to demonstrate rigour, show impact, and clearly narrate improvement.
The classroom, in the current context, is a situated arrangement of learners (IB MYP/DP), concepts (schema/stereotype), worksheets, boards, desks, expectations, and assessments. Situated learning theory helps explain why meaning cannot be detached from the terms of participation in which it emerges (Clancey, 1995).
The classroom encounters, discussed here, involve vulnerability, anonymity, and interpretation. Allowing for relational traces of pedagogical life that demand care in how they are represented and reread (Noddings, 1984; Palmer, 1998; Ergas, 2018).

---

### Reflective Investigation

## a. Identifying the Issue

The evidence for this essay consists primarily of post-lesson reflections and critical incident reports gathered in the professional development portfolio and curated through Tauira. These materials are useful because they make visible the structure of prescribed reflection. The template does not simply ask what happened in a lesson; it already organises response into what was successful, what should change, and what this means for personal growth. The issue, then, is not only what I say in reflection, but how the form of reflection pre-narrates what legitimate growth should look like.



## b. Intervention and Inquiry

The task at hand was to review three classroom encounters. First, each encounter was examined through the classic reflective models such as Gibbs, Kolb, and Schön. The purpose was not to reject reflective models altogether, but to assess what they make effortless to say and what they make challenging to notice. Second, one encounter was reread diffractively through Tauira. 
In the first encounter, a lesson on affordance appeared strong during the planning phase. Nonetheless, the classroom lost energy when students shifted from conceptual understanding to applying creative design. When read with Gibbs or Schön, this encounter could be narrated as a pacing issue and therefore as an opportunity for better future adjustment (Gibbs, 1988; Schön, 1983). However, when read diffractively, the same encounter was perceived differently. The students’ worksheet directed attention toward correctness. The lesson sequence favoured analytic performance. The desks arranged in traditional rows oriented students toward paper and screen. My own desire for visible evidence of learning intensified micro-management. The problem was not with my technique for facilitating learning experiences. Instead, an assemblage had created a mode of participation in which students could satisfy without entering a thorough relation with the task or one another.
The second encounter involved a written homework task. I learned that a student regularly created informational content on YouTube. My immediate reflective note recognised this as differentiation and student-centred planning. Again, conventional reflective models could translate the moment into a positive story of responsiveness and professional growth (Gibbs, 1988; Schön, 1983). As expected, the diffractive account of the encounter unsettled this neat translation. The encounter exposed how strongly I default to written prose as the apt medium of seriousness, rigour, and assessable understanding. The pedagogical shift, therefore, was not simply from one homework format to another. It involved a reconfiguration of validity, medium, assessment, and my own pedagogical comfort. Constructivist and situated accounts of learning help explain that knowledge is not neutral with respect to the forms in which it is produced and demonstrated, and disciplinary participation can be enabled or constrained by the media that institutions value (Clancey, 1995; Bada and Olusegun, 2015; Peden and VanVoorhis, 2023).
The third encounter took place during a lesson on schema, stereotype, and culture. A student recognised that her personal view had been shaped by social and cultural conditioning. This led to confusion and sadness, an emotional turmoil. A conventional reflective cycle could help me look at this encounter as one requiring sensitivity, care, and improved facilitation of learning experiences. Conversely, a diffractive reading resisted reducing it to a better future technique. The sadness in the room emerged through concept, self-awareness, identity, memory, classroom tempo, institutional expectations, and my own unstable roles as educator, witness, caretaker, and researcher. What appeared, when read diffractively, was a pedagogical threshold in which learning happened through discomfort, affect, and relational exposure rather than through cognitive mastery alone (Meyer and Land, 2003; Meyer and Land, 2006; Noddings, 1984).
At this point, Tauira made a difference because it allowed the encounter to be mapped relationally rather than summarised retrospectively. Figure 1 brings together the three encounters and the possible relations mapped around sadness within encounter (cluster) three. The figure is useful because it makes visible the density of connections through which the encounter took shape.

Within Cluster 3, the mapped co-participants were categorised as material (M), knowledge (K), and instincts (I). The co-participants are represented by the nodes (green, yellow, and purple dots) as in Tauira (see figure 2).  Figure 3 made the hidden four attributes of the third encounter visible. First, the concentration of force around sadness in the cluster is because several relations converged around it. Second, the Schema and Stereotype Concept operated as the link between the lesson-as-designed and the lesson-as-lived. The concept traversed into the student’s affective life through recognition that surpassed the planned academic task. Third, the cluster displayed two parallel tracks. One track connected board language, conceptual recognition, sadness, and role instability.  The other track connected worksheet structure and classroom tempo. Oddly, these tracks were coexisting without being sufficiently integrated. This means the lesson kept moving, while the affective event unfolded on a different spatiotemporal plane. Fourth, Role Instability appeared as an unresolved line of flight, suggesting that the educator-researcher’s ethical and professional positioning had been disrupted without being fully transformed.

The diffractive story does not end here, as another wave entirely enters this apparatus. A wave that the apparatus was not designed to receive. Students encounter the concept of stereotype not as an abstract category but as a description of what they have personally lived and experienced without being aware of it. Simultaneously, student identity enters from the biographical histories students carry in their bodies, such as the cultural memories, the embodied experiences of being stereotyped, the costs of recognition, and an entirely different direction.  Both the concept and student identity converge into sadness. Here is where the interference pattern emerges. Two waves (one curricular, Schema/Stereotype Concept, arriving from Board Language and one biographical, student identity, arriving from outside the apparatus entirely) pass through Sadness. Neither wave alone would have produced what emerges. The curriculum without student identity would have remained an academic exercise. Student identity without the curriculum would have stayed private, unaddressed in the classroom space. It is only at this intersection where the material, knowledge, and instinct meet that Sadness becomes possible, necessary, and real.
I do not consider this encounter a teaching failure. This is not an unintended side effect. In Barad's framework, this is the only phenomenon, at least for the current analysis, that was happening in the room (Barad, 2007). The lesson did not accidentally produce sadness, as the lesson was always already an encounter between conceptual frames and lived bodies. Sadness is the pattern that interference makes visible.
What the diffractive reading then demands attention to is what happens downstream of this interference, and its implications for me. Sadness does not dissolve into the lesson. It does not become an assessment output. It does not enter the Analytic Worksheet. It cannot because there is no edge from Sadness to Track B (see Figure 3). Instead, Sadness fires a single outgoing disruption into role instability. The educator-researcher, who stood in the room as an educator, a witness, a caretaker, and a researcher simultaneously, finds all four of those roles made incommensurable in a single moment. The teaching role says, “continue the lesson”. The witness role says, “stop and acknowledge”. The caretaker role says, “handle this carefully”. The researcher's role says, “record what you are seeing”. None of these can be fully enacted at the same time. Role instability, then, is the correct response to an impossible co-presence of ethical and professional practitioner demands.
These findings are supported conceptually by diffractive methodology, ecological accounts of relational environment, and work on interaction-dominant systems. Diffractive methodology helps explain why the event should not be reduced to an educator observing a student from outside the phenomenon (Barad, 2007; Bozalek and Zembylas, 2017). Ecological and affordance-based literature helps explain why classroom arrangements, artefacts, and action possibilities matter as co-creators of what could happen (Gibson, 2014; Maier and Fadel, 2009; Read and Szokolszky, 2020). Work on complex and interaction-dominant systems further supports a non-linear perspective in which the lesson cannot be understood as a simple chain of causes located within individual minds alone (Wallot and Kelty-Stephen, 2018; Strom and Viesca, 2023).



## c. Professional Learning

Across these encounters and specifically the diffractive reading, my professional learning has shifted from seeing reflection as retrospective self-correction toward understanding it as rereading entangled pedagogical events. Kolb, Gibbs, and Schön remain useful because they help organise experience and return the practitioner to practice with discipline. But they also tend to position the educator as the central focus of the reflective account. In contrast, diffraction made it harder to narrate growth as a tidy sequence of noticing, adjusting, and improving.
What I learned about teaching, through the diffractive way of reflecting on the encounters, is that pedagogy is never only cognitive, never only human, and never fully contained by reflective templates. What I learned about myself is that my own professional habits and practice are shaped by institutional desires for evidence, clarity, validity, and control. Growth, then, is the disruption of the very narrative through which I had learned to recognise myself as a “good” reflective educator.


---

## Implications

The implications of this inquiry for me as an educator-researcher are fourfold. First, for learning, it suggests that meaningful learning is not exhausted by visible performance or conceptually correct responses. Affect, recognition, uncertainty, and medium also matter. This is consistent with constructivist, situated, and threshold accounts of learning, all of which resist reducing knowledge to discrete outcomes detached from the terms of participation (Clancey, 1995; Bada and Olusegun, 2015; Meyer and Land, 2006). For my practice, it means I need to design learning experiences with greater attention to relation, materiality, and the affective consequences of pedagogical decisions rather than relying only on retrospective adjustment.
Second, for pedagogy, it suggests that design must attend more carefully to materiality and affect. Classroom tasks, room arrangements, representational modes, and time structures are not neutral to teaching apparatus. 
Third, for reflective systems, it suggests that educators should not only ask what worked and what they would change, but also what relations, assumptions, and institutional pressures shaped the classroom encounter in the first place. This matters for leadership as well as reflection. Fullan (2002) argues that effective leadership generates intrinsic motivation rather than external compliance, and that externally defined goals and actions tend to produce only short-term, less durable engagement. In that sense, prescribed reflective routines are uncertain in securing evidence of professionalism without necessarily triggering deeper professional commitment in research inquiry. If reflection is to support meaningful growth, it must do more than organise compliance with institutional expectations. It must help generate internally committed engagement with the complex conditions of teaching and learning life.
Fourth, for future practice, Tauira offers a way of extending reflection into ongoing professional inquiry. By connecting encounters, artefacts, memos, and maps, reflection becomes an ongoing, real-time professional inquiry rather than a mere collection of archived evidence. This aligns with evidence-informed practice in a broader sense, but it also resists reducing evidence to what can be easily standardised or counted.


---

## Conclusion

This essay has argued with evidence that prescribed reflective practices support professional learning by scripting how personal growth should be narrated. By rereading portfolio evidence through Tauira and through a diffractive framework, I have tried to show that pedagogical experience exceeds that containment. It emerges through relations among bodies, concepts, objects, affects, timings, media, and institutional forms.
To reflect and to narrate growth otherwise is not to abandon reflection. It is to resist reducing professional growth to a neat story told after the lesson. Read through Fullan, the point is to cultivate ways of professional learning, such as Tauira. From this perspective, the work of reflection becomes less about proving that I have improved and more about learning how teaching and the educator are continually being made within entangled pedagogical life.


---

/memos/memo-001.title: Memo 001 — The Slowing of the Room
/memos/memo-001.content:
This memo responds to [[enc-2025-T1-W3-L2]], the encounter in which the worksheet-compliance and relational-thinning clusters became analytically visible. The compliance pattern traced here recurs in [[enc-2025-T1-W5-L3]] and the affective dimension connects to the legitimacy disturbance mapped in [[memo-002]].

## Gap: Time Pressure
The encounter identifies the worksheet, desks, analytic sequencing, and my desire for visible thinking, but the temporal pressure of the lesson is still not fully drawn into the assemblage. The need to complete, evidence, and move onward may have shaped the room before the slowing became visible. What looked like a weak transition may therefore have been mediated by the felt authority of lesson time itself.
A further gap lies in the creative task. I marked the move from conceptual understanding to creative design as the point where the room slowed, but I did not yet ask what kind of uncertainty the creative task introduced into an environment already organised around analytic clarity and correctness. In Tauira, this matters because the creative task may recur elsewhere as a threshold where pedagogical control weakens and other relations become possible. This threshold logic surfaces more fully in [[enc-2025-T1-W5-L3]] and [[memo-003]].

## Diffractive Reading 1 — Barad

Read through Barad, the event loses the simplicity of teacher action followed by student response. The slowing was not mine, theirs, or the task's alone. It emerged through the intra-action of worksheet, desks, bodies, sequencing, completion pressure, and my own orientation toward visible evidence. No single element stands outside the event as its master cause.

This matters for rhizomatic analysis because the scene can now connect outward to other Tauira nodes: visible evidence, analytic performance, compliance, and pedagogical tempo. The encounter becomes less a lesson about pacing and more a map of how rigour, material arrangement, and institutional timing repeatedly produce relational thinning. That same Baradian reading is applied to legitimacy in [[memo-002]] and to the concept-affect threshold in [[memo-003]].

## Diffractive Reading 2 — Massumi

Read through Massumi, the drop in energy can be understood as a shift in affective intensity rather than only a decline in engagement. The room did not stop working; it changed register. Curiosity thinned, compliance thickened, and bodies remained with the task without fully remaining with one another.

This reframes the encounter productively. Instead of asking only how I should improve the transition next time, Tauira allows the scene to be read as one instance in a wider affective pattern where institutional forms redirect intensity away from relation and toward evidence. That outward link is what makes the encounter rhizomatic rather than merely reflective. The same affective redistribution is traced in [[enc-2025-T1-W4-L1]] through the lens of medium and recognition, and in [[enc-2025-T1-W5-L3]] through the concept-sadness threshold.

/memos/memo-002.title: Memo 002 — Writing, Video, and the Legitimacy of Form
/memos/memo-002.content:
This memo responds to [[enc-2025-T1-W4-L1]], the encounter in which the writing-rigour, medium-recognition, and assessment-comfort clusters became visible. The legitimacy question it raises connects backward to the compliance patterns of [[enc-2025-T1-W3-L2]] analysed in [[memo-001]], and forward to the role-instability threshold of [[enc-2025-T1-W5-L3]] analysed in [[memo-003]].

## Gap: Naming Absence

In the encounter, I noted that the student regularly created informational content on YouTube, and I treated that as a clue toward a different mode of learning. Yet the platform itself remains under-analysed. It is present only as "video," not as an ecology of editing, audience, performance, circulation, and self-fashioning. If Tauira is to support rhizomatic analysis, then YouTube should be mapped not simply as a medium but as a participant in the pedagogical assemblage.

A second gap concerns assessment structure. I recognised that writing felt more measurable, academic, and institutionally legible to me, but I did not sufficiently analyse the criteria, habits, or inherited evaluative logics that make writing appear stable in the first place. This gap matters because the encounter is not only about student choice. It is also about the systems that secure one form as normal and cast another as a risk. The institutional grip of writing as evidence is the same force that produces compliance in [[enc-2025-T1-W3-L2]] and holds the lesson moving in [[enc-2025-T1-W5-L3]] even as sadness opens another temporality.

## Diffractive Reading 1 — Barad

Read through Barad, the move from written paragraph to video submission is no longer reducible to my flexibility as a teacher. The event emerges through the intra-action of student capability, platform familiarity, writing as institutional norm, assessment expectation, and my own comfort with textual evidence. What appears as adaptation is also a reconfiguration of legitimacy.

This reading helps the encounter travel rhizomatically across Tauira. It links to other nodes around visible rigour, institutional legibility, medium, and pedagogical authority, showing that the event is not unique but part of a broader pattern in which form silently governs what counts as learning. The same Baradian framework is applied to material compliance in [[memo-001]] and to the concept-affect intra-action in [[memo-003]].

## Diffractive Reading 2 — Massumi

Read through Massumi, the affective contrast in the scene becomes analytically useful. The student's enthusiasm and my discomfort were not simply emotions attached to different preferences. They were intensities moving through the task and redistributing where confidence, recognition, and authority were felt.

This matters because the task changed shape affectively before it changed shape pedagogically. The assignment became charged by recognition for the student and by uncertainty for me. Tauira can hold that tension as a recurring pattern: when alternative media enter the room, legitimacy is not just debated conceptually but felt through bodies, habits, and assessment anxieties. This affective redistribution of authority connects to the relational thinning of [[enc-2025-T1-W3-L2]] and to the sadness-threshold of [[enc-2025-T1-W5-L3]], both of which are held as affective events rather than procedural problems in [[memo-001]] and [[memo-003]].

/memos/memo-003.title: Memo 003 — Concept, Sadness, and the Affective Threshold
/memos/memo-003.content:
This memo responds to [[enc-2025-T1-W5-L3]], the encounter in which the concept-affect threshold, worksheet-tempo, and role-instability clusters became visible. The threshold logic it maps connects backward through [[enc-2025-T1-W3-L2]] and [[enc-2025-T1-W4-L1]] as earlier moments where institutional form and affective intensity came into tension. The diffractive readings here extend the frameworks applied in [[memo-001]] and [[memo-002]].

## Gap: Inherited Worlds

The encounter names schema, stereotype, culture, and the student's sadness, but the cultural histories that entered the room remain more implied than mapped. The sadness did not arise from concept alone. It emerged because the concept touched inherited worlds already living in memory, identity, and social belonging. Tauira should therefore trace this scene not only through the learner and the concept, but through the diffuse histories that made recognition costly.

A second gap concerns the worksheet and board. Both remained in place as the sadness emerged, yet I have not sufficiently analysed how they sustained the lesson's analytical momentum even as another layer of time opened in the room. Their persistence matters because they help show how institutional pedagogy can continue moving while affect interrupts it from within. This worksheet-as-anchor pattern was already visible in [[enc-2025-T1-W3-L2]] and is theorised through Barad in [[memo-001]].

## Diffractive Reading 1 — Barad

Read through Barad, the sadness is not best understood as a private student reaction to an abstract concept. It emerges through the intra-action of concept, identity, worksheet, board language, lesson tempo, my unstable responsibilities, and the institutional demand that the lesson remain pedagogically legible. The event is therefore irreducibly relational.

This shifts the encounter within Tauira from a cautionary classroom moment to a dense analytic node. It now connects outward to other sites where concept becomes affect, where analytical structures hold while emotional thresholds emerge, and where teacher identity becomes unstable inside the lesson rather than after it. That wider connectivity links to the institutional legitimacy patterns of [[enc-2025-T1-W4-L1]] and [[memo-002]], and to the compliance-affect assemblage of [[enc-2025-T1-W3-L2]] and [[memo-001]].

## Diffractive Reading 2 — Massumi

Read through Massumi, the student's sadness can be approached as a threshold event. Cognition tipped into intensity, and that intensity moved through the room before any response could fully manage or narrate it. The room's atmosphere changed not because a lesson objective failed, but because learning exceeded the tempo set for it.

This is precisely the kind of moment prescribed reflection struggles to hold. It can be translated into a future action point about sensitivity, but Tauira allows it to remain more open: a pedagogical threshold where concept, affect, ethics, and temporality became inseparable. In rhizomatic terms, sadness here is not an interruption outside learning. It is one pathway through which learning happened. The same pathway — learning exceeding its institutional tempo — is what thinned relation in [[enc-2025-T1-W3-L2]] and redistributed affective authority in [[enc-2025-T1-W4-L1]].
